findings.title: Recitation and the audience-side barrier
findings.claim: The focus pairs Qur'an recitation with a hidden barrier between two parties. Wider scenes let that barrier resonate as a relation of uptake: speakers name a veil between themselves and the addressee alongside covered hearts and heavy ears, while other passages describe failed understanding and deliberate interference with listening.
findings.mechanism: The focus's two between-poles and حجابًا return in 41:5 as بيننا وبينك حجاب, with the speakers also locating covering in their hearts and heaviness in their ears. In 6:25, people listen while heart-covers prevent understanding and ears carry weight; 41:26 depicts an instruction to avoid listening to the Qur'an and make noise within it, while 8:23 leaves turning away present even if hearing is granted. These contacts give the screen a reception-side effect alongside its stated placement between the reciter and the named group.
findings.reader_payoff: The barrier can be perceived both as a between-speakers partition and as a boundary around hearing and understanding, with divine placement, hearer self-description, and deliberate refusal held together.
findings.containment: These are separate passages and do not identify the same hearers or decide how divine placement, disposition, and deliberate interference relate. In 17:45 itself, God places a hidden barrier between the reciter and those who do not believe in the Hereafter.

epistemic.reason: The originating reader walk is legacy_unbound. The bounded relation is independently grounded by the exact focus surface and supplied connection Arabic; external morphology and root identities are not inferred.

findings.title: Other responses to recitation
findings.claim: Wider recitation scenes also show listeners who are told to attend in silence and listeners who carry a warning onward. Beside the focus's barrier for a named audience, these responses keep Qur'anic recitation open to distinct forms of reception.
findings.mechanism: The supplied Arabic of 7:204 pairs Qur'an recitation with listening and silence so mercy may follow; in 46:29, a group listens to the Qur'an, asks one another for silence, then returns to warn its people. The repeated act of recitation contacts the focus's conditional scene, making its barrier particular to the named hearers rather than a property assigned to every encounter.
findings.reader_payoff: The recitation can be seen as a common address with different receptions, while the focus keeps its attention on those who reject the Hereafter.
findings.containment: These are separate audiences and do not establish that the focus's hearers receive or evade the barrier. The focus still states that a hidden barrier is placed between the reciter and its named group.

epistemic.reason: The connection rows supply exact Arabic with explicit recitation, listening, silence, and subsequent warning or mercy; the inference is limited to distinct reception patterns.

findings.title: The veil as a regulated threshold
findings.claim: Across wider uses, a حجاب can mark a boundary that structures contact: speech may occur from behind it, a request may be made from behind it, and other encounters unfold within a veiled scene.
findings.mechanism: The focus's حجابًا returns in 42:51 as one mode behind which divine speech occurs, in 33:53 as the position from which a request is made, and in 19:17 and 7:46 in scenes of separation with encounter or address still present. This wider usage brings a mediated-threshold resonance back through the focus's veil word.
findings.reader_payoff: The focus's screen can be felt as a relational boundary whose effect depends on the parties and the form of contact, while its separation of reciter and deniers remains clear.
findings.containment: The other scenes do not identify the focus's audience or establish that its deniers receive the recitation. They show only that the wider veil image can structure communication as well as separation; the focus does not specify such passage.

epistemic.reason: The focus branch is accepted and the supplied target Arabic visibly repeats حجاب, but target morphology is absent; the finding stays at contextual surface and relation level.

findings.title: Recitation beside refuge
findings.claim: A wider recitation echo pairs the same Qur'an-reading condition with a command to seek God's protection, allowing the hidden boundary in 17:45 to carry a secondary protective resonance alongside separation.
findings.mechanism: The focus's إذا قرأت القرآن is repeated in 16:98 before the command to seek refuge in God from Satan. Because the same act of recitation precedes the focus's veil, the external command lends the veil a protective edge without stating its purpose.
findings.reader_payoff: The moment of recitation can be sensed as an occasion of refuge as well as a between-speakers boundary.
findings.containment: 16:98 explicitly commands seeking refuge; 17:45 does not equate that refuge with its veil or state why the barrier is placed. The protective note remains a secondary resonance.

epistemic.reason: The repeated recitation phrase and refuge command are explicit in supplied Arabic, while connecting the focus's veil to protection is an indirect, bounded inference.

findings.title: The named audience's wider response
findings.claim: The focus's phrase for those who do not believe in the Hereafter recurs beside recoil when God alone is mentioned and altered appraisal of deeds, giving the audience label a wider profile of active response.
findings.mechanism: The supplied Arabic of 39:45 repeats the focus's description and associates it with hearts recoiling at mention of God alone; 27:4 repeats the description beside deeds made attractive and bewilderment. The exact audience phrase returns through the focus's belief and Hereafter words, changing the label from a bare category into a wider pattern of response and valuation.
findings.reader_payoff: The people between whom the barrier is placed can be perceived through a wider relation to divine mention and judgment, not only through a stated position about the Hereafter.
findings.containment: These are parallel descriptions, not proof of identical audiences or of reactions caused by the recitation in 17:45. The focus does not itself state recoil or altered appraisal.

epistemic.reason: The audience phrase and its contextual responses are explicit in supplied Arabic, but the external passages have no morphology joins and are retained only as contextual resonance.
